articles.title: China broke free trade, answer isn’t tariffs
articles.summary: Mind Field News: All wars aren’t fought with guns and bombs. The biggest ones of our time have weaponised tariffs, export bans and tech transfer curbs. We call these w.
articles.body: All wars aren’t fought with guns and bombs. The biggest ones of our time have weaponised tariffs, export bans and tech transfer curbs. We call these wars trade wars. But make no mistake, they aren’t being fought over dollars and cents. The goal, yet again, is hegemony. Question is why, after a 70-year free-trade consensus, world’s turned to trade tribalism. Also, if trade wars are unavoidable, how do you win them? Soumaya Keynes and Chad P Bown have some answers in their book, How to Win a Trade War: An Optimistic Guide to an Anxious Global Economy.Since public memory is short, Trump seems the obvious culprit, for he’s fixated on tariffs from the start of his second term last year. But Keynes, a Financial Times columnist, and Bown, chief economist with US State Dept under Biden, say it was China that really broke the rules-based order that underpinned free trade. Key to that old world – the authors are convinced it’s irretrievably lost – was the willingness to be interdependent. But the ‘Made in China 2025’ policy upended that system in 2015 with a clear aim to dominate important industrial sectors of the future with market share targets, they say. Then came the ‘Dual Circulation’ strategy, clearly intended to end Chinese dependence on the rest of the world while increasing other nations’ dependence on it.China got there, Keynes and Bown say, by turning off the safety switch of economic systems. Ordinarily, overproduction leads to a price crash, which penalises further production. But in China, overproduction is rewarded. That’s why Europe’s car industry, for example, is in a crisis. European buyers are getting cheap Chinese cars that German or French carmakers can’t compete with on price. This is an existential threat for Europe’s biggest industry. And other industries across the world are in the same spot. Which means jobs, social stability and national security are at risk. Hence, the authors say, more trade wars are inevitable.But that does not mean tariffing everyone like Trump, because “import barriers are like party drugs, with an initial rush and then a comedown”. China’s strategy of starving rivals of key inputs also has its limitations: “export controls are like trying to keep an unruly teenager indoors”. Keynes and Bown cite the example of 19th-century Britain’s control over telegraph cables. Britain wasn’t letting Germany build a parallel network, so Germany found an answer in wireless radio. Likewise, whether it’s America’s control on advanced chips or China’s control on rare earths, they’ll work only in the short term.To really win a trade war, Keynes and Bown say, start by preparing the key players: govt, companies and people. Why people? Because trade is never a people’s priority. “In Brexit, just 6% of Britons thought their country would benefit in terms of trade and economy by being outside EU.” And when simple things like toys and asthma inhalers – imported, of course – start getting expensive, people lose all their zeal for a trade war.To prep seriously, identify your vulnerabilities, and use subsidies to produce what you can, and stockpile what you can’t. Only then wade into the war, taking care not to alienate your allies. The authors say victory in a trade war is pyrrhic, but you’ll know you won if you “lose less than your rival” and “minimise” your wounds.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. May we continue to stand by one another as we build a safer and more affordable city for all,” he said.His Rakshabandhan message comes as Mamdani continues to emphasise community, affordability and safety as key themes of his political agenda in New York. articles.title: Iceland heads to the polls in knife-edge vote on restarting EU talks
articles.summary: Amid economic and security challenges, Iceland is holding a referendum more than a decade after pausing accession talks.
articles.body:
Icelanders head to the polls on Saturday to decide whether their country should reenter negotiations to join the European Union, a vote that could have economic and security implications beyond the small Arctic country.

The election comes 13 years after Iceland, under a Eurosceptic government, paused the last EU accession talks, believing the country would fare better outside the bloc.

Arctic security concerns have grown amid Russia’s war against Ukraine and United States President Donald Trump’s threats to invade neighbouring Greenland, the cost of living has climbed and Iceland’s currency has kept wavering.

Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir, whose Social Democrats party is pro-EU, said she will honour whatever choice the public makes.

If Icelanders vote “yes”, the country would likely start years of negotiations with Brussels to hammer out membership terms. It would then hold a second referendum on whether to formally become part of the EU.

Frostadottir has said a “yes” vote would see the nation “enter negotiations with our heads held high and stand together in seeking a good agreement”.

If the result is “no”, “all speculation about what [EU membership] might involve will be set aside”, she said.

Recent surveys show Icelanders are almost evenly split on the proposal.

A Gallup opinion poll conducted this week found that 51.6 percent of respondents were against new EU membership talks, while 48.4 percent favoured them.

An earlier survey by Icelandic pollster Maskina showed a narrow majority of 51.3 percent of respondents backing new EU accession talks.

Gabriella Gricius, associate professor of strategy at the Norwegian Military Academy, said Iceland’s lack of armed forces has always left it “reliant on NATO and specifically the US for its security”.

“As the US has grown more unpredictable, and specifically, its rhetoric around Greenland has grown more concerning, it is not surprising that Iceland is seeking additional security guarantees through the EU,” Gricius told Al Jazeera.

Adam Fishwick, a lecturer in international relations at the University of Iceland, said the expected benefits of membership would be reduced inflation, a more stable currency and fewer customs barriers for consumers.

“There may also be opportunities for regional development in Iceland, which is an important issue here, with access to dedicated EU funds,” he told Al Jazeera.

However, the debate over EU accession remains “quite polarised”, he noted. Opponents fear the small nation of 395,000 people would “lose control over everyday policy decisions” and have limited sway in a bloc filled with larger European powers, Fishwick said.

Voters to weigh impact on inflation, currency

The benefits of EU membership for Iceland are not as obvious as for other potential candidates.

Iceland is a relatively wealthy country that, as a member of Schengen and the European Economic Area, already gets a lot of the single-market access that would come with EU membership.

However, the country has experienced growing economic pains in recent years, primarily regarding the cost of living. Consumer prices in 2025 exceeded those of any EU state and were 87 percent higher than the EU average.

Iceland’s currency, the krona, meanwhile, has been prone to exchange-rate swings that opponents say lower investment confidence and make it more costly to borrow money. Earlier this year, the Ministry of Finance and Economic Affairs concluded that the costs of maintaining Iceland’s own currency probably outweigh the benefits. Adopting the euro, it said in a report, may help reduce interest rates and transaction costs.

Joining the EU could help address both issues.

Iceland would become a part of the bloc’s customs union, in which goods move freely between members and face a common tariff when imported from non-member countries. It could also adopt the more stable euro as its currency.

Fishing industry concerns: ‘Backbone of the economy’

A major concern, though, is the impact on the country’s fishing industry, an economic pillar that in 2024 directly contributed about 8 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and much more indirectly.

By joining the EU, Iceland would become subject to the EU’s Common Fisheries Policy, which governs European fishing fleets and fish stocks.

Iceland’s fishing industry fears this change could lead to new catch quotas, increased foreign competition and, more broadly, less control over local fishing policy.

“The fundamental objection to EU membership is that Iceland would not retain full control over its fisheries – the traditional backbone of the economy,” Valur Ingimundarson, professor of contemporary history at the University of Iceland, told Al Jazeera.

Even if Icelanders vote “yes” to proceed with EU negotiations, the country is unlikely to go forward with EU membership unless it secures “ironclad” exemptions regarding its fishing industry, said Ingimundarson.

Mounting security pressures in the Arctic, coupled with uncertainty about US commitment to its traditional European partners, are also contributing to Iceland’s renewed interest in the EU, say analysts.

Though Iceland is a founding member of NATO and has a 75-year defence treaty with the US, it has no standing armed forces of its own and is located in a geopolitical hotspot that both Russia and the US have sought to project power in.

While Russia has expanded its military presence in the Arctic in recent years, President Trump has repeatedly threatened to use force to seize nearby Greenland.

Ingimundarson said pro-EU Icelanders see “the EU as a source of political and economic protection for a small state confronted by coercive great-power politics and uncertainty about the US as a reliable security partner”.

Iceland’s Foreign Minister Thorgerdur Gunnarsdottir has said membership would be “a valuable addition” for Iceland, even though NATO and the US would still be its core security partners.

In comments to Reuters, Gunnarsdottir said Iceland has been “disappointed” with the US’s “pressure campaign waged against both Greenlanders and Denmark”.

Russia poses a security threat “in our waters and nearby, in the North Atlantic”, said Gunnarsdottir.

For the EU, bringing Iceland into its orbit would expand EU territory much deeper into the North Atlantic, potentially deepening its strategic focus there, said Gricius, the professor.

“Icelandic membership in the EU wouldn’t necessarily change Arctic security dynamics, as Iceland is and will continue to be an Arctic state,” she said. “However, it may influence how the EU behaves in the Arctic, as the EU would then include four of the eight Arctic states – Iceland, Finland, Sweden and Denmark.”

articles.title: ‘Ab ghar wali chai bhi Taj Hotel ke rate wali’: Mumbai milk price jumps ₹9, leaving social media users angry, amused and sarcastic
articles.summary: Trending News: A cup of morning tea may soon cost a little more to make in Mumbai. The Bombay Milk Producers’ Association has raised the wholesale price of buffalo m.
articles.body: A cup of morning tea may soon cost a little more to make in Mumbai. The Bombay Milk Producers’ Association has raised the wholesale price of buffalo milk from ₹93 to ₹102 per litre, effective September 1. The revised rate will remain in place until February 28, 2027. Retail prices are expected to rise accordingly.For families buying milk every day, even a ₹9 increase can feel bigger than it looks on paper. And that is exactly what many social media reactions reflect.‘Now even chai will feel expensive’On X and Instagram, the response quickly moved beyond the price itself. Some users complained about another hit to household budgets, while others turned the hike into jokes.One Instagram user quipped that after sugar and milk, even a simple cup of tea could start feeling like a luxury. Another sarcastically asked whether milk was now travelling through the Strait of Hormuz.There were also political comments, jokes about inflation and suggestions to switch to cow milk. Some users simply posted laughing emojis.Beneath the humour, however, sits a familiar worry: daily-use items are becoming harder to ignore in household spending.Why has milk become ₹9 costlier?The producers have pointed to rising input costs.Association president CK Singh said the prices of several feed ingredients, including grain, tuvar chuni, chana chuni and corn, have risen by up to 25%. Grass and fodder have also become more expensive.The association said the increase was necessary because producers could not continue selling at the old rate. Members unanimously approved the revision.That explanation matters because milk prices do not depend only on the milk itself. The cost of keeping the animal healthy, feeding it and maintaining the dairy operation eventually travels through the supply chain.This is not the only recent milk hikeMumbai consumers have already seen another dairy price increase this month.Maharashtra’s Gokul raised its buffalo milk retail price by ₹2 per litre, taking the one-litre pouch to ₹78 in Mumbai and Pune. The cooperative also increased the procurement price paid to farmers.So the latest ₹9 wholesale increase is arriving after another recent revision.Sugar has already made Mumbai households nervousMumbai sugar prices also rose sharply in August. TOI reported that retail sugar prices in parts of the city jumped from ₹50 to ₹58 per kg in a week, with traders expecting further increases at the time.The Centre later said sugar prices nationally had risen from ₹48.18 per kg on July 20 to ₹55.70 on August 20, an increase of about 15.6%. It attributed the recent rise to factors including lower-than-expected production, festive demand, weather-related crop damage, tighter global supplies and speculation or hoarding.For a household, these numbers rarely remain separate. Milk goes into tea, curd, sweets and desserts. Sugar goes into the same tea and many festive preparations. That is why a price increase of ₹9 can create a reaction far larger than ₹9.Disclaimer: Prices and market conditions can change quickly. articles.title: Drumcree: A parades commission in crisis
articles.summary: In the late 1990s, the Drumcree parade cranked up tensions to levels felt during the worst of the Troubles, resulting in murders, riots, and roadblocks.
articles.body:
A largely forgotten Orange Order marching dispute, from one of the darkest periods of Northern Ireland's past, has thrown the Parades Commission into crisis.

It has also picked at old wounds, re-igniting arguments about rights and respect in a divided society.

In the late 1990s, the Drumcree parade cranked up tensions to levels felt during the worst of the Troubles, resulting in murders, riots, and roadblocks.

The issue, if not officially settled, had been in a coma until Tuesday's High Court outcome.

The parade takes place in Portadown every July on the Sunday before the Twelfth.

Since 1998, and from its creation, the Parades Commission has imposed restrictions on the local the Orange lodge's route back from a service at Drumcree Church.

It prevents marchers from setting foot on the mainly Nationalist Garvaghy Road – the flashpoint of previous summers.

The ban is also imposed on very small weekly parades from the church in protest, which stop at a police line at a distance from Garvaghy Road.

For the lodge and supporters, the 1998 parade remains unfinished and each application seeks its completion.

The Orange Order and Unionism have never fully embraced the Parades Commission, which they have always perceived as being biased against them.

This has played into the fall-out from the High Court case and the calls for resignations or dismissals.

Legal disclosure flushed out some internal communications which reflect badly on the six government-appointed commissioners.

As pressure grew, one of them, Billy Gamble, resigned on Thursday.

The commissioners' salaries, when added together, are in the region of £180,000 a year for working one or two days per week.

The case revealed that not all of them had signed off on the final determination before it was issued, although they said they had all agreed imposing the restrictions.

In quashing their determination, Mr Justice McAlinden was scathing in his observations, referring to "sloppy procedures" and "shortcuts".

The public body has been damaged and it is ultimately for the new Secretary of State, Sir Chris Bryant, to ensure the rebuilding of confidence in it.

Will sackings be required in the absence of any further resignations?

Is a review of other determinations needed?

As he himself put it, it is "a priority issue".

He will have heard the united position of unionist parties who want all the commissioners replaced.

Bryant will also have noted that First Minister Michelle O'Neill visited Garvaghy Road within 24 hours of the court case and said there is "anxiety" amongst residents over any parade.

Whether a parade will now be permitted is a different matter – the High Court did not authorise one.

There will be a new parade application requiring a fresh decision, one which will need to be watertight procedurally and able to withstand any further judicial tests.

The Orange Order is buoyed by success at court and a march date in late September is being discussed.

While it won the case, because the commission conceded before a full hearing, the court did not have to make a ruling on the wider grounds of the challenge.

This included a claim that the commission has wrongly made dialogue between the Orange Order and residents a pre-requisite of any parade.

The Orange Order has requested talks, but they have been knocked back.

Breandan Mac Cionnaith of the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition told BBC News NI: "What is the point of having any talks if there is a pre-determined outcome?

"It is 28 years since the last march came down the road.

"Who wants to open that can of worms again?"

Nigel Dawson, Portadown District Master of the Orange Order, said it is up for mediation.

But he accepted it would engage "to support our application" to march, adding: "The focus has always been to bring our bannerette home from Drumcree in 1998."

The court case has upped the ante around the next application, which is imminent.

The decision will be awaited with greater anticipation than the hundreds of times it has been made over the last three decades.

articles.title: Six months into the Iran war, a new Gulf security architecture is emerging
articles.summary: Gulf states are building overlapping partnerships that complement, rather than replace, the US security role.
articles.body:
Six months into the war with Iran, it is worth taking stock of what has actually changed around the Gulf.

After Iran’s June 2025 missile strike on Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, I argued that the years ahead would be more perilous for the Gulf and that deeper defence cooperation and integration would eventually become unavoidable. Earlier this month, I wrote here that the Gulf could no longer rely entirely on the old security toolkit and would need to build more of a security ecosystem of its own. So far, events have borne out the broad direction of both arguments.

What has become clearer over the past six months is that the war is not simply changing defence budgets or generating new security agreements. It is beginning to change how Gulf states think about security itself: who they should work with, what they should expect from their partners and what cooperation needs to look like when a crisis actually begins.

Some of these changes are obvious. The war has demonstrated, in the most direct possible way, the vulnerability of cities, energy infrastructure, airports, ports and shipping lanes to missiles, drones and other forms of disruption. Threats that were often discussed in exercises and planning documents have become immediate operational problems.

For decades, Gulf security rested on a familiar structure: the United States provided the main external security umbrella, Gulf states maintained bilateral relationships with Washington and other Western capitals, and the GCC provided a regional framework in which defence integration remained uneven.

That system has not disappeared. Nor should it. The US remains indispensable to Gulf security and will continue to play a central role for the foreseeable future. What is changing is the assumption that this structure, by itself, is enough.

The war has accelerated the move towards a more layered security system. Gulf states are strengthening cooperation among themselves while deepening relationships with a wider range of partners. Turkiye is becoming more important. European states have greater potential to play an operational role. Existing bilateral military relationships are being asked to deliver more, while new regional arrangements are emerging alongside older ones.

The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement between Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan is perhaps the clearest recent example. Its declaration that an armed attack on one would be treated as an attack on all immediately invited comparisons with NATO.

The principle itself is not new to Gulf security. The GCC’s existing Joint Defence Agreement already treats an attack on one member as an attack on all, a commitment GCC states have repeatedly reaffirmed during the current war. What makes the Mecca agreement different is that it extends this collective-defence logic beyond the GCC, linking Saudi Arabia to Turkiye and Pakistan.

The comparison with NATO is understandable, but it can also distract from what is actually happening. The Gulf does not need to reproduce NATO, nor is the wider Middle East particularly suited to one large security alliance built around a single hierarchy and a single understanding of threat.

The threat facing a Gulf state may come from a state one day and a non-state actor the next. Countries that see one threat in much the same way may have very different views of another. And no regional state, however capable, is likely to be accepted as the permanent political and military leader of every possible coalition.

What appears to be emerging instead is a system of overlapping partnerships rather than one grand alliance. Different countries will work together against different threats. Some arrangements will be Gulf-led; others will bring in regional or Western partners.

Such a system also requires a different way of thinking about leadership. A regional security architecture built around permanent hierarchy will always face resistance. Gulf and Middle Eastern states are protective of their sovereignty and bring very different capabilities to the table.

Leadership should therefore follow the threat. The state facing the immediate danger should have the leading political voice in setting the objectives of the response, the acceptable level of escalation and the use of its territory. But operational leadership need not mirror political hierarchy.

A maritime crisis may be best handled by the partner with the strongest naval capability. An air defence crisis may require the partner with the most relevant capabilities to take a larger operational role.

This kind of flexibility may be the only realistic basis for deeper security cooperation. But it depends on whether these overlapping relationships can connect when they need to.

This is where interoperability becomes important. If several countries agree that they will support one another in a crisis, can they actually do it? Can they share information quickly, communicate across their militaries, coordinate decisions and know in advance who is authorised to do what?

An attack on one country does not necessarily mean every partner must respond in exactly the same way. Support can take many forms, from intelligence, air defence and logistics to maritime protection or, in the most serious circumstances, direct military action. The clearer these expectations are before a crisis, the more credible the commitment becomes when one occurs.

There are already examples of what deeper integration can look like without requiring a large regional institution. Qatar’s military relationship with Britain has gone beyond the traditional buyer-seller model. British and Qatari personnel have trained and operated Typhoon aircraft together through the joint squadron, while Qatar and Turkiye have developed a combined military command structure.

These arrangements predate the current war. The UK-Qatar relationship, however, was also tested during it: in March, an RAF Typhoon operating with the joint squadron shot down an Iranian attack drone directed at Qatar.

Integration does not always have to begin with a treaty signed by ten countries. Sometimes it begins with two militaries learning how to work together properly.

Europe can play a larger role without replacing the US. Washington will likely remain the Gulf’s most important security partner while Gulf states build deeper operational relationships with Britain, France, Turkiye and other capable partners.

The past six months have strengthened the case for doing so. Gulf and European militaries increasingly face many of the same operational problems: missiles, drones, maritime insecurity, electronic warfare and threats to critical infrastructure. The next stage of Gulf-European defence relations should therefore be judged less by the value of contracts signed and more by whether their forces can actually work together when circumstances require it.

That means more exercises, embedded personnel and joint planning, as well as arrangements that allow bilateral partnerships to connect with wider GCC and regional structures.

The Mecca agreement will face the same test. Turkiye’s defence ministry has said that the three countries plan political and military coordination, joint exercises, air-defence cooperation and deeper defence-industrial ties.

For now, however, these remain plans rather than proof of operational integration. The agreement’s significance will ultimately depend on whether Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani forces develop habits of cooperation: whether they can share intelligence, coordinate air defence, sustain operations together and use defence-industrial cooperation to solve practical military problems.

Six months into the Iran war, then, the outlines of a different Gulf security architecture are beginning to appear.

It is unlikely to consist of one alliance, one leader or one definition of the threat. Nor is the Gulf abandoning the US or dismantling the security relationships that have served it for decades. Instead, a more flexible system is taking shape around these existing relationships: stronger Gulf cooperation, additional regional partnerships, deeper links with European militaries and a greater emphasis on whether countries can actually operate together.

Some of this momentum may fade if the immediate threat recedes. The challenge now is to make the lessons of the past six months durable. Ultimately, the test remains a simple one. When the next missile is launched, the next drone crosses a border or the next shipping lane comes under threat, can the countries concerned see the danger together, make decisions together and respond together?

If they can, then the most important legacy of this war may not be another treaty or another alliance. It may be the beginning of a Gulf security system that is more connected, more flexible and better suited to the region it is actually meant to protect.

articles.body:
Artists are being encouraged to put themselves forward for a public art project.

Torridge District Council has asked for expressions of interest from people keen to create an original artwork for and about Westward Ho! in Devon.

Councillor Claire Hodson said the piece of art "has the potential to become a valued landmark in the village, fostering pride among residents and offering a fresh cultural experience for our visitors".

articles.title: Lanydrock puts dress made for turn of the century goes on display
articles.summary: The Cockleshell Dress, designed to welcome in the 20th Century, is on display for a month.
articles.body:
A dress designed to welcome in the 20th Century has gone on display for a month at a country house.

The Cockleshell Dress was worn by Mary Vere Agar-Robartes, the eldest daughter of Thomas Charles Reginald Agar-Robartes and Mary Dickinson, who lived at Lanhydrock, near Bodmin, Cornwall, from 1879 to 1946.

The dress - made from cream silk and decorated with a shell pattern, gold-thread detailing and a commemorative sash bearing the date 1900 - was restored by the National Trust's textiles conservators.

Nicola Heald, from the trust, said the dress would only be exhibited between 28 August to 27 September "because the fabric is so sensitive to light" and the display was a "rare chance" to see it.

Heald, the collections and house manager, said: "It's a real treat to be able to put the Cockleshell Dress on display.

"Because the fabric is so sensitive to light, opportunities to see it are very limited, so this month-long display gives visitors a rare chance to appreciate the detail and craftsmanship of the dress up close."

She said the design of the dress was thought to have been inspired by the nursery rhyme Mary, Mary, Quite Contrary due to its reference to "silver bells and cockle shells".

"This wasn't simply a beautiful dress, it was something Mary wore to celebrate the arrival of a new century, and it helps bring that moment in the family's story to life," she said.

articles.title: 'I've visited 50 places on extreme day trips'
articles.summary: Claire Howard has spent the day on the beaches of Benidorm and eating Italian food in Bergamo.
articles.body:
A woman has become hooked on extreme day-tripping, flying to about 50 destinations from Birmingham Airport.

An extreme day trip is a travel trend where someone travels to a destination in a different country and returns home the same day.

Claire Howard, a teacher from Solihull, told BBC CWR that she has spent the day on the beaches of Benidorm, listening to French live music in Beauvais and eating Italian food in Bergamo.

She said: "I have seen more places for less money and go to places I would never have been to."

Howard began embarking on day trips from Birmingham after her friend bagged them both £29 return tickets to Dublin for the day for her birthday around two and half years ago.

She got a taste for it and decided to see where else she can go within 12 to 24 hours.

The furthest she has travelled in a day is to Malaga, about a two-and-a-half-hour flight. For beginners she advises heading to destinations such as Dublin, Belfast or Edinburgh.

Howard told BBC CWR that she sometimes flies out on a Monday evening, books a cheap hostel, has the full day in the destination the next day, flies home in the evening and is back in work by Wednesday.

Howard said she spends around £150 all-in for a day trip which includes transport, food and parking.

"I wouldn't try to do a whole city in a day, pick one or two things you really want to see and just wander", she added.

She was aware of the environmental impact of extreme day tripping but she tries to be sustainable in other areas of her life, she said.

"For the past year I have only bought second-hand clothes," she said.

"All forms of holiday, like cruise ships, have an environmental impact, but we all try to offset that where we can and live our lives."

Out of the near 50 extreme day trips Howard has embarked on, she said she has only ever had one bad experience when her return flight was cancelled.

She said: "I feel tired when I come home but you feel like you have done something kind of incredible.

"You might have been somewhere like the top of Mont Blanc and then the next day you are back in work – you just feel like you have done something really cool."

articles.title: Courteeners: From humble Manchester roots to the world - and back
articles.summary: Courteeners frontman Liam Fray revisits the Manchester pub where he first got on stage in 2005.
articles.body:
The street outside legendary indie club 42s, a front garden on Burnage Lane and a pub's function room with a tiny stage - all locations in Manchester where you could have found Courteeners in their early days.

The four school friends from Middleton, near Rochdale, have certainly come a long way since they hit the Manchester indie scene in 2006.

While they have travelled around the world ever since, there is no place like home and they will take to the stage later for a huge homecoming gig at Wythenshawe Park.

From humble beginnings performing for friends in the garden of their shared house in Burnage, the Courteeners are now celebrating 20 years together.

Fresh from releasing a new best-of compilation album called God Bless The Band, lead singer and songwriter Liam Fray spoke to BBC North West Tonight at The Briton's Protection pub on Deansgate, where he first performed as a solo artist back in 2005.

Sitting upstairs in the pub, Fray smiled at the 3ft (2m) stage and single spotlight on the ceiling while recalling the night he spent there more than two decades ago.

"It's unusual to be in here and it's exactly the same," he said. "It is very small."

Fray recalled the gig, the crowd of 80, and of how - determined to make it big - he had bought every ticket himself and went on to sell them to fellow indie fans.

"I went the morning the tickets went on sale and bought them all so that it said 'Sold Out'," Fray remembered.

"I took them to 42s and sold them all on the dance floor."

The Not Nineteen Forever songwriter said he had played a few of his early gigs at the venue and was joined by drummer Michael Campbell, who would eventually his Courteeners bandmate.

"When I played here with Campbell I'm pretty sure we oversold it by about 100 people," Fray said.

"The people who ran it at the time tried to get to the stage to stop us performing but they couldn't get to us.

"Everyone who was with us now was in that room."

He said despite now performing gigs across the globe, he still "feels close" to the old days.

"It's mad that it's been 20 years," Fray said. "Because we still feel young.

"There are definitely moments where I'm playing Acrylic or Bide Your Time and I think we did that in my parents' garage in 2004.

"It was a long time ago, and people are still discovering these songs… [I feel] blessed, absolutely blessed."

On the release of the band's greatest hits record, which features songs from each of their seven albums, Fray said he had found himself looking back over the years.

"It's a lifetime since we started this band," he explained. "The one thing we've got - that maybe people aren't as lucky to have - is that we are all so close to each other."

The original band members were Fray, Campbell, Daniel Moores and Mark Cuppello.

They have been described as friends from the age of 10, with later members Joe Cross and Elina Lin respectively joining the band in 2015 and 2019.

"We didn't answer an advert in the paper. We've been friends so long and were friends before we were a band," Fray said of the group's chemistry. "You always felt dead safe in a unit."

The gig at Wythenshawe Park will see Courteeners perform in front of up to 35,000 fans.

Support acts include Merseyside band The Coral and The Vaccines.

Fray said it would be his first visit to Wythenshawe Park and he was "more ready than ever".

He added: "Just getting that many people together and singing songs, they're not our songs anymore... they're theirs.

"To be stood up there, it's like I want to pat my mates on the back because they've done a great job.

"It's not been a super smooth ride but I'm going to take in every second."

Organisers of Wythenshawe Live said £1 from each ticket sold would be given to the Music Venue Trust, a charity which fights to improve and protect grassroots music venues in the UK.

Fray said he remained dedicated to helping such venues and upcoming artists.

"It didn't happen to us overnight and one day we are playing Heaton Park," he explained.

"There were lots of Dry Bars in there, lots of Night and Day [in Manchester], HiFi Club in Leeds, The Magnet in Liverpool.

"They make you who you are. They're your scars, they're your war wounds.

articles.title: Bangladesh's search for modern fighter ends with Chinese J-10; should India be worried?
articles.summary: International News: Bangladesh is moving closer to becoming the second confirmed export customer for China's J-10CE fighter jet, in a development that is being watched cl.
articles.body: Bangladesh is moving closer to becoming the second confirmed export customer for China's J-10CE fighter jet, in a development that is being watched closely in New Delhi. A government panel in Dhaka is preparing a draft agreement to open formal negotiations with Beijing for the aircraft. If it goes through, the deal would rank among Bangladesh's biggest defence procurements in years and further deepen its military relationship with China, already Dhaka's largest arms supplier.Local media has been reporting that Bangladesh is looking to acquire up to 24 J-10CE jets, with earlier estimates from October last year pegging the cost of the airframes alone at around USD1.2 billion. The complete aircraft package, including weapons, spares and training, will be closer to USD2.2 billion. Payments as per the same reports were expected to be spread across a decade, running until 2035-36, as part of Bangladesh's broader Forces Goal 2030 modernisation plan aimed at replacing its ageing fleet of Chengdu F-7s and MiG-29s.What makes this development particularly significant is the reasoning behind it. Rahman was candid in pointing to the J-10CE's performance during last year's clashes between India and Pakistan, where Islamabad claimed the jet was used to down Indian fighters, claims India continues to dispute. Pakistan remains the only confirmed operator of the export variant so far, having inducted the aircraft in 2022, but the reported combat record appears to have shifted Dhaka's calculus meaningfully.This is not Bangladesh's first attempt at procuring a modern fighter aircraft, having been exploring the option since 2024, while also weighing the French Rafale and, more recently, signing a Letter of Intent for the Eurofighter Typhoon. The Bangladeshi air force is seeking a modern aircraft under a programme titled 'Forces Goal 2030'. The aim of the project is to improve the combat capabilities of the Bangladeshi armed forces across the spectrum. The last aircraft procured by the Bangladeshi air force was the Chinese origin F-7, which itself is a derivative of the MiG-21. The Bangladeshis have not been able to procure a western fighter aircraft due to financial constraints. Bangladesh had in December signed a Letter of Intent with the Italian firm Leonardo to procure the Eurofighter Typhoon.For India, the implications are straightforward but uncomfortable. A second South Asian air force operating the same Chinese jet already in Pakistani service would give Bangladesh its first credible beyond-visual-range combat capability, backed by a modern AESA radar and networked systems, right along India's eastern border, more crucially along the Siliguri border. It also underscores Beijing's expanding footprint in South Asia's defence landscape, with China yet to lock in a second confirmed J-10CE customer anywhere else in the world despite interest from countries including Egypt, Indonesia and Iran, making Bangladesh's potential purchase a genuine milestone in China's fighter export ambitions.This move also comes at a time when China's share of the global defence market has dropped according to a report by Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI). China's defence exports have dropped despite the fact that the global arms procurement has increased in the same time, partially buoyed by increased arms procurement by Europe in response to the conflict in Ukraine. A significant portion of China's defence exports head to Pakistan, with Bangladesh also having a small share of Chinese exports.

articles.title: Nagendra resigned to avoid embarrassment to Congress: DK Shivakumar
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Karnataka chief minister DK Shivakumar said on Saturday that B Nagendra, who held the planning and statistics portfolio, has submitted his .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Karnataka chief minister DK Shivakumar said on Saturday that B Nagendra, who held the planning and statistics portfolio, has submitted his resignation from the state cabinet to avoid embarrassment to the Congress party, though the final decision will be taken after discussions with the party high command.Nagendra resigned from the state Cabinet on Friday as opposition protested over his alleged involvement in the Rs 89 crore Valmiki Corporation scam, marking his second resignation, 25 days after being re-inducted on August 3."Minister Nagendra has submitted his resignation to avoid embarrassment to the party. After discussing with the party high command, a final decision will be taken tomorrow morning," Shivakumar said.According to Shivakumar, Nagendra submitted his resignation after being hurt by opposition’s "false allegations" and the disruption of Assembly proceedings, highlighting his role as "a Dalit and Scheduled Caste leader" who defeated senior BJP leaders in elections."Though Nagendra has handed over his resignation letter, it will be brought to the notice of the Congress high command in Delhi, and after discussing with them, a final decision will be taken," he said."Nagendra is innocent. After verifying the investigation reports and after discussion, it is known that there is no truth in the allegations against him," he said, adding that the manner in which the BJP had treated a Dalit leader had hurt the wider poor population.The opposition BJP, which along with ally JD(S), has been demanding for the Ballary rural MLA’s sacking ever since he made his way back into the Cabinet, described his stepping down as a "victory"."Today I am voluntarily tendering my resignation as minister," Nagendra said on Friday as he broke down in tears in front of the reportersNagendra compared himself being targeted to Lord Ram’s killing of Shambuka in Ramayana, alleging that the "manuwadis" never want a tribal person to rise.According to the Uttara Kand of Ramayana, ascetic Shambuka was killed by Rama for performing penance.He claimed that his name had been included in the second charge sheet filed by the central agencies, and that it was not included in the first CBI charge sheet.Nagendra thanked several party leaders like Shivakumar, Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge, Rahul Gandhi, and Siddaramaiah for extending support to him, stating he voluntarily resigned despite repeated assurances from the party leaders.Nagendra also said he would travel across Karnataka, including the 15 Assembly constituencies reserved for Scheduled Tribes, to highlight the alleged injustice.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1832, a New York merchant built a house with a hidden 2-foot-wide passage; researchers now link it to the Underground Railroad
articles.summary: US News: For decades, visitors to Manhattan's Merchant's House Museum walked past a built-in chest of drawers without knowing the full significance of the narr.
articles.body: For decades, visitors to Manhattan's Merchant's House Museum walked past a built-in chest of drawers without knowing the full significance of the narrow passage concealed behind it. After two years of research, historians concluded that the passage was likely used as a hiding place for people escaping slavery. The passage is roughly 2 feet square and descends about 15 feet from the second floor toward the ground floor. The museum announced the finding in February 2026, describing the 1832 Merchant's House as the earliest known site of Underground Railroad activity in New York City. The house was built by Joseph Brewster, a wealthy merchant and abolitionist, and the museum says the passage appears to have been incorporated into the building when it was constructed. Its physical existence was known before the recent research; what changed was the understanding of what the unusual space may have been used for.Why historians believe the passage was connected to the Underground RailroadAccording to the Merchant's House Museum, the passage is an unusual feature of the 1832 building and has no obvious domestic purpose. Its entrance is concealed beneath a built-in chest of drawers on the second floor, while the narrow shaft extends downward through the house. Researchers examined the architecture alongside historical evidence about Brewster and New York's abolitionist movement. Patrick Ciccone, an architectural historian involved in the research, emphasised that Brewster's background was significant because wealthy white New Yorkers who openly opposed slavery were unusual at the time. He described Brewster as the builder of the house, meaning he was in a position to make deliberate choices about its construction. The museum has therefore interpreted the passage as a space intended to conceal freedom-seekers, while continuing to distinguish that conclusion from a surviving document that explicitly states who used the passage or exactly how often it was used.Why the discovery adds another chapter to New York's abolitionist historyThe passage was constructed during a complicated period in New York. Although New York State had abolished slavery in 1827, the city's economy remained closely connected to the slaveholding South. At the same time, New York had an active abolitionist movement led in large part by free Black residents, alongside white abolitionists who worked within the movement. People involved in helping those escaping slavery often had to operate discreetly. The Underground Railroad was not a literal railroad but a loose network of people, homes and other locations that helped freedom-seekers travel toward places where they could live outside the institution of slavery. The Merchant's House passage provides a rare physical reminder of that history. Much of what is known about the Underground Railroad comes from documentary accounts, oral histories and later historical research. Intact spaces that may have been used for concealment are considerably rarer.How the hidden passage survived inside the Merchant's HouseThe Merchant's House was constructed in 1832 and later became the home of the Tredwell family, who occupied the property for almost a century. The building eventually became a museum in 1936 and is now one of New York City's best-preserved examples of a 19th-century merchant family's home. The concealed passage survived largely intact within the building. Its entrance is hidden beneath a chest of drawers, making it difficult to notice as part of the house's ordinary interior. The recent research brought together the physical evidence inside the building with historical information about Brewster and the abolitionist networks operating in New York during the period. The museum subsequently presented the passage as evidence of the house's connection to the Underground Railroad.What the discovery means for ManhattanThe Merchant's House Museum now identifies the property as the earliest known Underground Railroad site in New York City. That distinction is significant because Manhattan played an important role in the abolitionist movement, yet comparatively few physical spaces associated with the city's Underground Railroad history have survived in an intact form. The discovery also broadens the story told by the museum itself. For decades, the Merchant's House was primarily understood through the domestic history of the Tredwell family and their household. The hidden passage adds another layer to that history, connecting the building to the wider struggle over slavery and freedom in 19th-century New York. For historians, the most important question may now be what else can be established about the passage. The architecture suggests a deliberate attempt at concealment, while Brewster's abolitionist views provide historical context. But identifying the specific people who may have sheltered there and documenting how the space was actually used will require further research.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1946, Eisenhower’s brothers gave their Abilene family home to a foundation; it opened to visitors the next year
articles.summary: US News: Ida Eisenhower died in 1946, when her six sons gave the family home in Abilene, Kansas, to the Eisenhower Foundation. The house opened to the public i.
articles.body: Ida Eisenhower died in 1946, when her six sons gave the family home in Abilene, Kansas, to the Eisenhower Foundation. The house opened to the public in June 1947 and was preserved with the furniture and household details that remained after their mother’s death. The house had been the Eisenhower family home since 1898. David and Ida Eisenhower bought the six-room property on Southeast Fourth Street from David’s brother, Abraham Lincoln Eisenhower, and raised their six sons there. Dwight D. Eisenhower, who later became the 34th president of the United States, lived in the house until he left for the U.S. Military Academy at West Point in 1911. According to the Eisenhower Presidential Library, the family remained in the house until Ida died in 1946.The house where six Eisenhower boys grew upThe property covered about 2.5 to 3 acres and included a barn, chicken house, smokehouse, outhouse, orchard, strawberry patch and kitchen garden. In 1900, Ida's father-in-law, Jacob Eisenhower, moved in with the family. Two bedrooms and a walk-through closet were added to the east side of the house, and an indoor bathroom was added around 1908, followed by a small kitchen, pantry and enclosed back porch in 1915. TheEisenhower Presidential Library records those changes in its history of the property.Dwight was one of the six brothers raised in the house. He left Abilene for West Point in 1911, but the rest of the family continued living there for decades. His father, David, died in 1942, and Ida remained in the house until her death four years later.The brothers decided to preserve the family homeAfter Ida's death, the house could have become another privately held family property; instead, the Eisenhower brothers agreed to give it to the Eisenhower Foundation, which had been established in 1945 to create a memorial to General Eisenhower and honor World War II veterans. The foundation's early records provide a more detailed account of the transfer. In its 1947 annual meeting report, the Kansas Historical Society recorded that Milton Eisenhower acted for the surviving brothers when the property was deeded to the foundation in June 1946. One of the six brothers, Arthur, had died in 1942.A new roof and paint were among the early repairs, and the primary intention was to preserve the rooms and possessions as they had been during Ida Eisenhower's lifetime. The decision meant visitors could see more than an old house associated with a future president. The furnishings, books, piano, kitchen equipment and bedroom furniture remained in place. The 1947 Kansas Historical Society account described the rooms as they had been left by Ida.Visitors arrived within monthsThe Eisenhower Foundation opened the house to the public on June 22, 1947. More than 500 people visited on the opening day, according to the Eisenhower Foundation, and the event was broadcast by seven radio stations. A Kansas Historical Society account published in 1947 said more than 12,000 people had toured the house during its first 120 days, with visitors arriving from every U.S. state and 11 foreign countries. The foundation hired guides to take visitors through the rooms.At that point, Eisenhower was still a military figure rather than a former president, and his presidency eventually began in January 1953, after he won the 1952 election. The house continued to be associated with him as his public career developed. It was eventually incorporated into the larger presidential library and museum complex in Abilene.The home survived a major floodIn July 1951, flooding damaged the basement and ruined part of its rock foundation. The first floor managed to escape the flood damage, but the structure needed substantial work. Repairs were completed several years later, and the home was rededicated in November 1956. The White House Historical Association notes that later maintenance, including work on climate and security systems, exterior painting and reroofing, has helped retain its appearance.The property was eventually transferred from the Eisenhower Foundation to the federal government in 1966 and became part of the presidential library system. The Texas Historical Commission also records that the foundation operated the house until the transfer. The Eisenhower Presidential Library says the house is furnished as it was when Ida died in 1946. Many of the furnishings are original, while some have been moved to accommodate visitors.A preservation project completed in 2022 included exterior lead-paint abatement and maintenance work. The home now provides scheduled tours from Tuesday through Sunday, with tours limited to 10 people at a time. The house at Southeast Fourth Street remains part of the Eisenhower Presidential Library, Museum and Boyhood Home in Abilene. The building where the Eisenhower family lived from 1898 until Ida's death in 1946 has been receiving visitors since 1947.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 1974, a biologist moved to a Washington island because one marsh supported 80 bird species; he devoted the rest of his life to it, and neighbours later created a wildlife preserve
articles.summary: US News: Discover how Dr. Frank Richardson transformed a marsh on Orcas Island into the Frank Richardson Wildfowl Preserve, protecting 80 bird species and inspiring generations through his commitment to wildlife conservation.
articles.body: When Dr. Frank Richardson retired from the University of Washington in 1972, he did not slow down. He shifted his fieldwork from museum collections to a wetland near his home, trading decades of specimen cataloguing for hours spent watching live birds in the marsh. Two years later, he made the shift permanent, settling on Orcas Island in the San Juan Islands and turning that single wetland into the last great subject of his working life. The marsh he studied now bears his name as a protected wildlife preserve, a legacy his neighbours created after his death.Richardson spent his career as a professor of zoology at the University of Washington and headed the ornithology division at the Burke Museum, which held one of the country's largest bird specimen collections. After stepping down from that post in 1972, he did not retire from birdwatching itself, spending time studying bird life on Cypress Island before settling permanently on Orcas Island in 1974 with his wife, Dorothy, the San Juan Preservation Trust, which now manages the reserve built around his work.Richardson's academic training left him with a habit of counting and cataloguing what he saw rather than simply observing it. Near Deer Harbour, he soon began studying a modest wetland close to his new home.An unusually busy patch of wetlandRichardson found that the marsh supported an unusually high number of bird species. Despite covering only a small stretch of land near Channel Road, the site supported roughly 80 different species of birds moving through or nesting there across the seasons, an unusually high count for a wetland of its size. The marsh sat along the Pacific Flyway, the migratory corridor that carries waterfowl and shorebirds up and down the West Coast each year. That helped explain why so many species stopped there.Richardson came to believe that counting birds alone was not enough. He had watched habitats disappear across the region during his academic career, and he concluded that the long-term survival of many species depended on protecting the specific pieces of ground they relied on, not just studying them from a distance. That conviction led him to land conservation work in the San Juan Islands during his final years, applying decades of ornithological training to protect a single marsh.A preserve built after his deathRichardson died in 1985, but his work to protect the marsh continued after his death. The following year, neighbours Bob and Meg Connor donated a seven-acre conservation easement covering the eastern portion of the wetland, a gift that initiated the effort to establish the Frank Richardson Wildfowl Preserve. A memorial plaque to Richardson now sits on a boulder along Channel Road at the edge of the marsh, marking the spot for visitors who stop to look out over the water.Richardson's influence on Orcas Island extended beyond the marsh itself. Colleagues remembered him as a generous mentor, including wildlife artist Tony Angell, who said a chance friendship with Richardson at the Burke Museum shaped his career studying and illustrating Northwest birds, as documented by HistoryLink, the Washington State history resource. Angell later credited those early outings with Richardson, searching for carving stone along the Upper Skagit and examining study skins at the museum, as the spark that led him to a lifetime of wildlife art.That same generosity was reflected in how Richardson was remembered professionally after he died in 1985. An obituary published the following year in The Auk, the journal of the American Ornithologists' Union, noted the breadth of Richardson's contributions to Pacific Northwest ornithology over a career that ultimately outlasted his formal retirement by well over a decade.Today the preserve remains a working wetland rather than a museum piece, still hosting the same seasonal traffic of migrating wildfowl that first caught Richardson's attention half a century ago. Part of its acreage lies in upland forest across the road from the marsh itself, and a short pedestrian path leads visitors up to a screened viewpoint overlooking the water. It is a small piece of ground by conservation standards, but it stands as the direct result of one retired professor's decision to keep doing fieldwork long after his job ended and of neighbours who chose to protect that work after he was gone.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Former Ecuadorian President Lenín Moreno sentenced to 5 years for corruption
articles.summary: Former Ecuadorian President Lenín Moreno was sentenced Friday to 5 years in prison after a court found him guilty of accepting bribes from a Chinese company in exchange for helping it secure a contract to build a hydroelectric plant.
articles.body: QUITO, Ecuador — Former Ecuadorian President Lenín Moreno was sentenced Friday to 5 years in prison after a court found him guilty of accepting bribes from a Chinese company in exchange for helping it secure a contract to build a hydroelectric plant. Moreno, who was present for the reading of the verdict, is 73 years old and has a physical disability that prevents him from walking. He will serve the sentence under house arrest. Moreno was convicted as a direct participant in the bribery scheme during his tenure as vice president under Rafael Correa. His wife and daughter, two brothers and a brother-in-law were convicted as accomplices. The wife and daughter each received 30-month sentences. All were ordered to repay triple what they received illicitly within a period of 90 days. Moreno is the third former Ecuadorian president to be sentenced for corruption, though he was tried for crimes before reaching the presidency. Correa was sentenced in 2020 to eight years in prison in a bribery case involving Brazilian construction giant Odebrecht but remains in Belgium, where he has lived for years. Former President Jamil Mahuad was also sentenced in 2014 to eight years for misuse of public funds. Another former president, Abdalá Bucaram, is awaiting sentencing after being convicted of organized crime. Prosecutors said a corruption network operated from 2008 to 2018, collecting bribes equal to 4% of the value of the project carried out by Sinohydro. They said the money was distributed through domestic and international transactions to public officials and other beneficiaries, including Moreno. Sinohydro began building the roughly $2 billion Coca Codo Sinclair hydroelectric plant in 2010 and handed it over to Ecuador in 2016. The project has since faced criticism over structural defects. Moreno, a tourism entrepreneur, rose to national prominence in 2007 when he became vice president under Correa, who governed Ecuador for a decade. Moreno served until 2013, when Jorge Glas succeeded him. In 2017, Moreno won the presidency as a candidate of the Correísta movement founded around Correa, with Glas as his running mate. Glas later left office and is now serving a prison sentence for corruption.

articles.title: Dutch health institute issues warning over Trump-shaped ecstasy pills
articles.summary: The drugs have a delayed effect which "increases the risk of overdose", the health institute says.
articles.body:
A Dutch drug addiction and mental health institute has issued a "red alert" to users about potentially lethal ecstasy pills which resemble US President Donald Trump.

The Utrecht-based Trimbos Institute said several of the pills had been handed in at testing centres in August and were found to contain a "very high" amount of the chemical PMMA.

"Do not use this pill under any circumstance," the institute said in its warning, cautioning that the drug could cause "overheating with potentially fatal consequences".

It issued images of the pills, which feature a depiction of Trump's face on one side and the words "Trump" and "NL" stamped on the other.

PMMA, or para-methoxymethamfetamine, is a substance similar to MDMA – the active ingredient in ecstasy pills.

"However, the effect occurs later, and the stimulating effect is often absent," the health institute advised. "This increases the risk of overdose."

Users are being warned they could experience symptoms such as nausea, an increased heart rate and convulsions hours after ingesting the pills.

Trimbos Institute spokesperson Anniek Groothuis told the Associated Press that it had no reported cases of death or serious illness among possible users.

While producing, selling and using ecstasy is illegal in the Netherlands, a 2024 Dutch government report said the substance was "still quite popular as a party drug".

The report added that, in 2022, a "record 550,000 people" had taken the drug at least once.

This is not the first time Donald Trump's facial features appear to have been used as inspiration for the shape of ecstasy pills.

In 2017, German police confiscated about 5,000 carrot-coloured ecstasy tablets in the shape of the US president's head – which they believed had been promoted on the internet under the slogan "Trump makes partying great again".

articles.title: Jersey solar panels: Rise in number of homes generating power
articles.summary: The use of solar panels and biofuel is on the rise across the island.
articles.body:
There has been a rise in the number of homes generating electricity, typically through solar panels, according to a government report.

The Jersey Energy Trends Report , which tracks trends in the island's energy supply, showed 99 more homes and businesses were generating electricity at the end of 2025 compared to the beginning of the same year.

There has also been an increase in use of biofuels as more firms and households are starting to more away from fossil fuels, the report shows.

Energy generated from the private site accounts for 3% of the island's overall supply, with the rest imported, the report states.

This is the first time the government tracked private homes.

Researchers found 641 private microgeneration sites by the end of 2025, up from 540 at the start of the same year when experts began monitoring.

Last year there were 2.4 GWh of electricity sold to Jersey Electricity for wider distribution as part of the public supply, according to the report.

This represented 5% of the electricity produced on the island and less than 0.5% of the total primary supply of electricity.

Of all the energy used, 37% was for residential use, 34% for predominantly road transportation and 29% for commercial, government and agriculture use.

Energy consumption by the commercial sector had remained largely level during the last five years. It dropped by 9% in the road sector, but had increased by 59% in the air and marine sector, the report stated.

articles.title: Nepal floods death toll climbs to 626, with 2,400 still missing as rescue efforts continue
articles.summary: The death toll from catastrophic flash floods and mudslides in Nepal rose to at least 626 on Saturday, as more than 2,400 people remained missing in the country, including around 90 Americans.
articles.body: The death toll from catastrophic flash floods and mudslides in Nepal rose to at least 626 on Saturday, as more than 2,400 people remained missing in the country, including around 90 Americans. Rescuers have struggled to reach devastated communities along the Nepal-Tibet border, with the scale of the disaster coming into view four days after the torrent of water, ice and debris swept through Himalayan valleys, destroying homes, bridges and other infrastructure. As families wait for news about their relatives, damaged roads, power outages and fears of further flooding have hampered rescue efforts. China has separately reported seven deaths and 554 people missing in its Tibet region, including hundreds of foreigners. It is unclear how much overlap there is between the Chinese and Nepali missing-person counts. The disaster began Wednesday when a massive chunk of ice and rock dozens of times larger than the Empire State Building broke off a mountaintop and triggered the catastrophic flooding, geologists said. Videos from the hardest-hit border regions showed people running as the debris flow swallowed buildings and vehicles, devastated towns and settlements, and severed roads, power and communications. The suspected collapse of a melting glacier shook the ground so violently that seismic monitors initially registered it as a magnitude-4.4 earthquake. The State Department said it is not aware of any confirmed American deaths, but the large number of U.S. citizens still unaccounted for has added to the growing uncertainty surrounding the disaster. Among the missing are Murphy, Texas residents Raghu Rajan and Archana Suresh. The pair were expected to cross the China-Nepal border Wednesday morning when the floods hit. Their phones last pinged that morning near a bridge that washed away. “We know the severity of it, but still, you know, there’s a ray of hope for us to find our loved ones,” Rajan’s sister-in-law Divya Chandrashekar told NBC Dallas-Fort Worth. Deepak and Madhu Ahuja, Plano, Texas business owners who have been married for 34 years, were in the area for a religious journey to Mount Kailash, a sacred site for both Hindus and Buddhists. Their family is now desperately trying to find them while holding out hope that they survived. “My first reaction was, ‘That cannot be true,’” Deepak’s brother Sushil Ahuja said. “They went there for a good cause, right? This cannot happen to them.” The State Department has urged U.S. citizens “currently in, or recently traveling through Rasuwa or another affected area” to get in touch via KathmanduACS@state.gov. A spokesperson said relatives seeking information about family members in Nepal “should call 1-888-407-4747 toll-free from the United States and Canada, or 1-202-501-4444 from other locations.” On Saturday, helicopters resumed operations in Nepal’s flood-hit Nuwakot district after poor weather temporarily halted efforts. Some helicopters arrived loaded with boxes and bags of aid, including clothes, instant noodles, crackers and rice, while others returned from the flood-hit areas carrying survivors, among them several babies from the nearby community of Trishuli. Scores of bodies recovered along the banks of the Trishuli and Narayani rivers have been brought to the city of Pokhara on Phewa Lake in central Nepal for identification. At the Western Regional Hospital in Pokhara, a crowd of families gathered Friday outside the facility’s morgue as they anxiously waited to see if their loved ones might be among the dead being brought to the medical facility. Inside the hospital, a digital display could be seen being set up to show photographs of the faces of some of the victims, in hopes that their loved ones might be able to identify them. The display was set up by police, with authorities saying some of the bodies recovered from the floods were in an advanced state of decomposition, making physical identification difficult. Meanwhile, rescuers are working “day and night” to search for survivors amid challenging conditions, a U.N. official said. “The government has established a relief fund, and already the World Bank, India, China and the U.S. have committed to pledge $229 million to support,” Lila Pieters Yahia, the U.N. resident coordinator in Nepal, said, adding that the U.N. is also providing $2 million from its humanitarian relief fund for immediate assistance. Nepal may need $4 billion to $5 billion to rebuild following the disaster, the country’s finance minister Swarnim Wagle told Reuters on Saturday.

articles.title: At least 27 dead and hundreds evacuated after strikes near Kyiv
articles.summary: The attack sparked a series of explosions, prompting an investigation into whether ammunition was being stored on site.
articles.body:
Twenty-seven people have been killed and almost 400 evacuated after a Russian strike hit a warehouse near Kyiv, triggering a fire and a series of explosions.

Regional governor Tymur Tkachenko said a further 42 people, including four children, were injured after the Russian drone strike in the Bucha district.

An investigation has been launched into whether ammunition was being stored at the site, where search and rescue operations were ongoing early on Saturday.

Meanwhile, Tkachenko said a 14-year-old was killed in a separate attack in the Boryspil district as President Volodymyr Zelensky reported overnight strikes across several regions.

In Russia, local officials say two people have been killed and 21 injured in strikes in the Belgorod and Rostov regions in the past 24 hours.

President Volodymyr Zelensky expressed his condolences to the families of the victims of the warehouse strike, saying that more than 300 emergency respondents had been deployed to the strike area.

He said an investigation into potential negligence had begun, writing on X: "The regulations are clear: ammunition must not be stored near houses or other residential buildings. Appropriate conclusions will certainly be drawn."

Russia's Ministry of Defence said in a statement that its forces had targeted "an ammunition depot" in the Kyiv region village of Myla, which stores "components and launch boosters for FP-1/FP-2 long-range unmanned aerial vehicles".

Zelensky also reported further overnight strikes in the regions of Odesa, Dnipropetrovsk, Sumy and Zaporizhzhia.

"Ukraine cannot be alone in finding solutions to protect against such strikes, and I thank everyone who helps with additional support packages and sanctions against Russia," he wrote on Telegram.

The Ukrainian army said it had shot down 233 Russia unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) overnight into Saturday.

Russia and Ukraine have been intensifying their attacks in recent months, with Kyiv focusing its operations on Russian economic targets.

Russian online retailer Ozon said one of its logistic centres had been hit in an overnight Ukrainian drone strike.

It said it had also suspended operations at a second logistics centre and evacuate staff "due to the danger in the area".

The retailer's facilities in Krasnodar, Dagestan, Stavropol and Adygea were targeted in strikes earlier this week, resulting in several injuries and widespread damage.

Ukraine has for weeks struck sites belonging to Wildberries, the country's biggest online retailer, describing the firm as a legitimate target because it supplied components to the military, which Moscow denies.

articles.title: She fled Iran. America sent her to Africa
articles.summary: “It’s okay now, I’m safe,” she remembered thinking. “I can make one new life here.”
articles.body: “It’s okay now, I’m safe,” she remembered thinking. “I can make one new life here.” She described her joy at reaching “one of the best countries in the world,” but her happiness would prove fleeting. Nika is among a growing number of migrants deported by the Trump administration to countries they’ve never been to – countries that can hardly be considered safe havens. It’s a loophole. Judges have stopped the US government from sending some migrants back to their home countries. So it has inked dozens of arrangements with third countries, where people like Nika are increasingly festering. Because she fears for both her and her family’s safety, Nika is a pseudonym. ‘If I was in Iran, they’re going to kill me’ Telling her story for the first time, Nika says she spent much of her youth protesting against the Iranian regime. “I lost too much of my friends. They [the Islamic Republic] killed them. And some of them are still in prison,” she said tearfully. “I know if I was in Iran, they’re going to kill me.” Her story unfolds at a remarkable time in US-Iran relations. Earlier this year, Iran was rocked by widespread anti-government protests. The regime launched an unprecedented crackdown, killing thousands. President Donald Trump encouraged protesters to “take over your institutions” and said, “help is on its way.” On the last day of February, the US and Israel launched a war on Iran, killing Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and attacking targets across the country. Nika followed the events closely from the United States. She allowed herself to hope it might mean the end of the Iranian regime, and a return home. In reality her fate had already been decided. One of the hardest days After being detained at the border and months in ICE detention, Nika had briefly been allowed to live freely in California. She received a Department of Homeland Security notice asking her to attend what she understood to be a routine meeting in June. But according to documents reviewed by CNN, US authorities had decided weeks earlier to deport her. When she attended the meeting, she was arrested. Three days later, on the evening of June 11, she says she was handcuffed, shackled and placed on a deportation flight along with 17 other migrants, including those from Afghanistan, Iraq and Georgia. “This is one of the very hard days in my life,” said Nika, describing how her whole body shook with fear. She said it was only on boarding the flight that she learned where she was going. The destination was shown on the small screen attached to the seat in front of her. Sahar Jalili Pawelski, Nika’s current immigration lawyer, said she tried desperately to get her off the flight. “I remember when the flight took off, I just sat on the floor, called my mom and cried. I live those moments. You know what that person must’ve been feeling. The loneliness she must have felt,” said Pawelski. Legal protection Like many of the other migrants she was deported with, Nika had won a protection order from an American judge. Such orders are intended to prevent migrants from being returned to places where they could face persecution, torture or death. Until recently, it was extremely rare for people with these types of protection orders to be deported. But since Trump returned to power last year, promising mass deportations, that’s all changed. Trump’s top anti-immigration advocate, deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, has stated “America’s doors are closed, fully, to asylum seekers.” The Department of Homeland Security has defended its actions, telling CNN in a statement that those deported received due process and had final orders of removal. “These third country agreements, which ensure due process under the U.S. Constitution, are essential to the safety of our homeland and the American people. We are applying the law as written. If a judge finds an illegal alien has no right to be in this country, we are going to remove them. Period.” Malaria and fear Since her arrival in the Central African Republic’s capital city of Bangui over two months ago, Nika says that she’s usually too scared to leave her apartment block and spends most of her time in her room. When she does go out to buy groceries or essentials, she claims the local police have often stopped her to demand bribes and threaten arrest if she doesn’t pay – claims the police denies. She’s also spent a stint at a local hospital, after contracting malaria. “I couldn’t believe I’m here,” Nika said. “Really, for me this is unbelievable.” The US State Department itself has advised against all travel to the country due to the risk of crime, kidnapping, disease and terrorism. It urges anyone who does make the journey to leave a DNA sample so they can be identified by their family in the event of their death. Why the Central African Republic agreed to accept migrants from the US is still something of a mystery. No details of the deal have been made public. But there are clues. This year the US has given a surprisingly large $85 million to the UN’s International Organization for Migration’s (IOM) operations in the Central African Republic, up from just a few million in previous years, as well as committing an additional $50 million to the country’s Humanitarian Fund. It comes at a time when the US is slashing foreign assistance. The State Department has hinted that that funding was a direct quid pro quo for accepting deportees. A DHS spokesperson told CNN that “the United States will use foreign assistance to support countries that help us achieve our immigration priorities.” The IOM, which does not facilitate deportations, did not reply to CNN’s specific questions but said in a statement it has a longstanding presence in the country. “As in other contexts, IOM benefits from funding from a range of donors in Central African Republic.” No one in the CAR’s government has spoken publicly about the deportation agreement, and rebuffed CNN’s requests for an interview. Life in limbo It’s unclear how life might unfold for Nika. She and the migrants she arrived with were told they were only being granted a temporary, three-month stay. A second deportation flight to the country left the US on July 31, this time carrying 31 deportees, and there’s a fear among the migrants that, as accommodation runs out, they will be forcibly repatriated to their countries of origin. If that were to happen, Nika does not rate her chances of survival. Her lawyer, meanwhile, is filing a federal lawsuit in an attempt to get her back to the US and re-open her claim for asylum. While Nika awaits her fate, she struggles to understand how the country she believed would protect her would be the one that sent her away.
