articles.title: Bombay HC disposes of plea by cab drivers as state govt grants 1-year time to learn Marathi language
articles.summary: MUMBAI: The Bombay high court has disposed of a petition challenging Maharashtra's Marathi language requirement for auto-rickshaw and taxi drivers aft.
articles.body: MUMBAI: The Bombay high court has disposed of a petition challenging Maharashtra's Marathi language requirement for auto-rickshaw and taxi drivers after the state government extended the deadline for learning the language by a year.The petition was filed by four cab drivers who had sought a stay on the implementation of the rule, arguing that it violated their fundamental rights.Additional government pleader Jyoti Chavan told a bench comprising acting Chief Justice Ravindra Ghuge and Justice Gautam Ankhad on Saturday that the government had decided to give drivers an additional year to acquire working knowledge of Marathi.The court accepted the government's statement and disposed of the petition.Chief minister Devendra Fadnavis announced the extension after a delegation of drivers met him on Thursday. The move means immediate action against non-Marathi-speaking drivers will be put on hold, giving them more time to learn the language.The public interest litigation (PIL), filed through advocate Vivek Shukla, challenged a government notification issued on 12 August, arguing that it violated citizens' fundamental rights.The petitioners – Mohd Kasim Ahmad, Mohd. Tauseef Shaikh, Siyad Ahamad and Sadik Nasir Ali Khan – said the rule violated their rights under Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution.They also argued that the requirement was beyond the powers granted to the state under the Motor Vehicles Act, which does not prescribe any language requirement for driving licences."The Motor Vehicles Act confers no power upon the State Government to prescribe working knowledge of any language as a qualification for a driver, as a condition of a badge, or as a condition of a permit, and confers no power to suspend or revoke a badge on such a ground," the plea had said.The petitioners said the rule threatened the livelihoods of lakhs of poor and migrant drivers, including themselves, because their badges could be suspended and permits cancelled for failing to demonstrate “working knowledge” of Marathi.They had asked the high court to stay the implementation of the rule.How the Marathi language rule unfoldedThe BJP-led Maharashtra government announced in April that drivers who did not speak Marathi would have to learn the basics of the language. A deadline of 15 August was set, with Marathi classes also organised for drivers.On 20 August, the transport department began checking commercial passenger vehicle drivers across the state, particularly auto-rickshaw and taxi drivers.Notices were issued to drivers who were found to lack adequate knowledge of Marathi. The action caused concern among thousands of non-native drivers and led to flash protests in some areas.Transport minister Pratap Sarnaik had said drivers who failed the Marathi test would be given one month to acquire working knowledge of the language.Those who failed to meet the requirement within that period would have their badges suspended for three months.The state government's decision to extend the deadline by another year has now brought an immediate legal challenge to the rule to an end.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: Trump admin seeks US Supreme Court nod for policy banning transgender from military service
articles.summary: US News: The Trump administration has asked the US Supreme Court to intervene in a legal battle over its policy banning transgender people from serving in the .
articles.body: The Trump administration has asked the US Supreme Court to intervene in a legal battle over its policy banning transgender people from serving in the military, seeking to clear the way for the discharge of about two dozen service members.According to The Washington Post, the administration has filed an emergency request seeking to lift a lower-court injunction that has allowed 28 transgender service members to remain in the military while their lawsuit challenging the policy proceeds.The case stems from an executive order signed by President Donald Trump shortly after he returned to office, directing the Pentagon to remove transgender service members. The Defence Department formally implemented the policy in February 2025.The administration argued that the executive branch has broad authority to determine military eligibility and that courts should defer to the Defence Department on questions of military readiness and effectiveness. Solicitor General D John Sauer urged the Supreme Court to intervene before the case reaches a full trial.The transgender service members, led by Army Reserve Second Lieutenant Nicolas Talbott, have argued that removing them before a final ruling would cause irreparable harm.In June, a divided three-judge panel of the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit upheld protections for the 28 service members, finding that the policy appeared to be driven by prejudice rather than military necessity.The administration's latest request marks a fresh escalation in the legal fight. The Supreme Court's conservative majority had previously allowed the administration to temporarily enforce the transgender military ban in an emergency ruling in May 2025.The Supreme Court is expected to decide this fall whether to take up the case for full review. If it agrees, a ruling could come during the court's upcoming term and potentially determine the constitutionality of Trump's transgender military policy.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Iceland votes on whether to restart talks on joining European Union
articles.summary: Icelanders voted on Saturday on whether to reopen membership talks with the European Union, with islanders split down the middle after a ⁠campaign focused on the cost of living, security, sovereignty and control over fishing waters.
articles.body: REYKJAVIK, Iceland — Icelanders voted on Saturday on whether to reopen membership talks with the European Union, with islanders split down the middle after a ⁠campaign focused on the cost of living, security, sovereignty and control over fishing waters. The race is too close to call. A Gallup poll on Friday suggested a narrow majority opposed reopening negotiations, a slight shift from earlier surveys that pointed to a narrow lead for supporters of renewed talks. “Yes” campaigners backing talks say joining the bloc could ease high interest rates and offer more security in a world unsettled by the war in Ukraine and U.S. President Donald Trump’s threats over ⁠another Arctic island, Greenland. “No” campaigners argue EU membership would threaten the island’s sovereignty ​and ⁠fishing waters. “Today is our encounter with history,” Iceland’s former President Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson, a campaigner against EU membership, said in a post on social media. Should voters say “yes”, that would only open the way to discussions with Brussels. Iceland would then have ⁠to hold a second referendum, likely several years later, on whether to join the EU. The European Union, comprising 27 member countries, is one of the world’s largest trading blocs. Alongside Norway and Switzerland, Iceland is one of a handful of northern and western European states to have long held out on joining, while Britain left the EU following its own referendum in 2016. Old questions, new urgency Iceland first applied to ​join the EU ⁠in 2009, amid a financial crisis that hit the ‌country’s small, exposed economy especially hard. Talks ended in 2013 when a Eurosceptic government shelved the process. Renewed geopolitical turmoil has brought fresh urgency to an issue Icelanders have debated on and off for decades. Foreign Minister Thorgerdur Katrin Gunnarsdottir, who has been backing ‘yes’, told Reuters last week ‌that Saturday’s vote boils down to a simple question: can Iceland still afford to stand ‌apart in a world where old certainties are crumbling? “The international order that underpinned our security and prosperity for decades is under serious pressure,” she said. “In times like these, small nations need to think carefully about where they stand and who stands with them.” High inflation Debates inside Iceland have focused more on interest rates, fishing rights ⁠and the cost of living than on security. Iceland has grappled with persistently high inflation and rates that made mortgages punishingly expensive, and supporters of a “yes” vote say EU membership, and possibly adoption of the euro, could offer some relief. Iceland’s central bank rate stands at 8.00%, against 2.25% at the European Central Bank. “It would not solve Iceland’s structural faults, but it could become a catalyst to a more healthy economy,” said Vilhjalmur Hilmarsson, chief economist at Viska, one of Iceland’s largest labour unions. Opposition leader Guðrún Hafsteinsdóttir, who has led the “no” campaign, has argued the economic case is overstated. “These are not problems that Brussels will solve for us. These are problems that Icelandic politicians must solve,” she said. Fishing a sticking point Under EU rules, fishing quotas are based on historical fishing patterns among other things. Some officials argue ​that would let Iceland keep control of its waters, since no EU country has fished there for decades. Opponents aren’t convinced. “I ‌know that the European Union will come up with some promises ⁠of some flexibility, especially in the beginning, but we know that it will not be for good,” Hafsteinsdóttir said. A foreign ministry ⁠memo estimates accession talks could start by the end of 2026 and take 18 to 24 months, if Saturday’s vote favours reopening negotiations. Iceland must also hold a general election ‌by November 2028, adding a further layer ​of political uncertainty to any negotiating timetable that stretches into that period. Polling ‌stations across the nation of roughly 400,000 ​people are due to close at 6 p.m. ET.

articles.title: 4 Arrested as Kenya Investigates 18 Elephant Deaths Near Amboseli
articles.summary: Four people have been arrested during an investigation into the deaths of 18 elephants in southern Kenya’s Amboseli ecosystem. The suspects have since been r...
articles.body:
Four people have been arrested during an investigation into the deaths of 18 elephants in southern Kenya's Amboseli ecosystem.

The suspects have since been released on bail, a Kenya Wildlife Service spokesperson told Reuters . The ministry has not announced their names or any formal charges.

The first 15 deaths were recorded between June 24 and July 24 in Amboseli National Park, Kimana Sanctuary and the Kuku Ranch area. The total had risen to 18 by August.

Preliminary laboratory findings point to a toxic substance as the cause of their deaths. An earlier theory suggested cyanide exposure through pesticide-contaminated tomatoes, but it has not been confirmed.

Four People Were Apprehended as Persons of Interest

Embedded media follows. Please allow a moment for it to load.

Kenya's Ministry of Tourism and Wildlife said the four were apprehended as persons of interest. Investigators are also looking for a fifth person believed to have information relevant to the case.

A search in Tikondo, Kimana, within Loitoktok Sub-County uncovered assorted chemicals and unlabeled materials. Some were believed to have entered Kenya from a neighboring country, and the recovered substances were sent for scientific testing.

The Tomato Explanation Is Still Only a Theory

Ten of the first 15 elephants showed similar symptoms, including partial paralysis that left them unable to stand. They died within one or two days. Most of the affected animals were adult females and calves, with only one adult male among the initial cases.

The Big Life Foundation said cyanide was detected in samples, but further testing was needed to determine whether the concentration was lethal. The conservation organization also said there was no clear evidence of where the substance came from or whether it was introduced intentionally.

Amboseli Is Famous for Its Elephant Herds

The Amboseli ecosystem includes the national park and surrounding community lands near Kenya's border with Tanzania. Elephants travel across that wider landscape beneath Mount Kilimanjaro rather than remaining inside the park.

Amboseli is one of Kenya's most popular safari destinations and is especially known for its large elephant herds. The Tourism and Wildlife Ministry's statement did not announce any visitor restrictions. The government said it is increasing wildlife surveillance, monitoring potentially hazardous substances and working with communities on both sides of the border.

articles.title: Sarah Ferguson expected back in the UK shortly, source tells BBC
articles.summary: The former Duchess of York is renting a six-bed house in the Home Counties, reports say.
articles.body:
The former Duchess of York is expected "back in the UK shortly", a source close to her has told the BBC.

Sarah Ferguson was thought to be living abroad after she was forced to move out of Royal Lodge in Windsor, which she shared with her ex-husband Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, in October.

Ferguson had last seen in public at the Duchess of Kent's funeral the previous month .

She is reportedly renting out a gated property in the Home Counties, according to the Sun newspaper.

Mountbatten-Windsor and Ferguson relinquished their royal titles following increased scrutiny and revelations surrounding their links to disgraced financier and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein .

'Marry me' and Epstein's 'baby boy' - key Sarah Ferguson revelations in emails

Ferguson is expected to move into the six-bedroom home "imminently", which could be as soon as next week, the Sun reported .

It is believed she has been spending her time out of the public eye at an Alpine chalet in Verbier, Switzerland, since leaving Royal Lodge. Her belongings were collected from Mountbatten-Windsor's home in Sandringham this week, the newspaper added.

She had been keeping a low profile since losing her titles alongside Mountbatten-Windsor after she became mired in the scandal about her connections to Epstein, and faced calls to speak to US authorities after last year's release of millions of documents shed new light on their relationship.

In one email exchange from 2011 , she appeared to privately apologise for her public rejection of Epstein, saying: "You have always been a steadfast, generous and supreme friend to me and my family."

A spokesperson for the duchess previously said the email was sent after Epstein had threatened to sue her for defamation - in an effort to convince him not to.

Another email suggested Ferguson took her daughters to see Epstein in the US days after he was released from prison for child sex crimes.

The emails do not indicate any wrongdoing.

Epstein was also ultimately the downfall of Mountbatten-Windsor, who was stripped of his titles by the King because of "serious lapses of judgment" over his friendship with the late paedophile. Mountbatten-Windsor has always denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein.

Ferguson lost her courtesy royal divorcee title and reverted to her maiden name, and also lost the freedom of the city of York after councillors voted unanimously to remove the honour over the scandal.

Her expected return comes just days after the Duke and Duchess of Sussex came back to Britain with their children to begin a new life after six years living in the US.

articles.title: IAEA: Low fuel stocks endanger occupied Ukrainian nuclear plant
articles.summary: The power supply to the Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhya Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) in Ukraine is critically endangered as fuel stocks for its emergency generat...
articles.body:
The power supply to the Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhya Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) in Ukraine is critically endangered as fuel stocks for its emergency generators dwindle, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) warned on Saturday.

The plant has now been without external power for more than a week and is reliant on the diesel generators, IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said.

It was reported that diesel supplies had temporarily been sufficient for only 10 days before several dozen tons of fuel were delivered from outside the site this week.

"The current situation once again shows why reliable external power and secure supply routes are indispensable for nuclear safety and security," said Grossi.

Without the restoration of the external power supply or additional deliveries of diesel in the near future, "the plant could face a station blackout within approximately 10 days," Grossi warned.

IAEA seeks local ceasefire for repair work

The IAEA is reportedly working to establish a zone for a localized ceasefire to enable repairs to a key power line. If successful, these repairs would restore the nuclear power station's external power supply.

The Zaporizhzhya plant, with six reactors, is the largest nuclear power plant in Europe. It came under Russian control shortly after the outbreak of the war in Ukraine in 2022 and has been struck multiple times since.

The reactors are shut down but must continue to be cooled. The IAEA has a permanent team on site to monitor the situation.

articles.title: In 1999, a Virginia couple founded a nonprofit riding programme for people with disabilities; after it became a USEF Center of Excellence, their historic 43-acre farm is listed for $8.4 million to fund future services
articles.summary: US News: What began as a family's search for meaningful opportunities for children with disabilities eventually grew into a nationally recognised equestrian pr.
articles.body: What began as a family's search for meaningful opportunities for children with disabilities eventually grew into a nationally recognised equestrian programme. In 1999, Mark and Muriel Forrest established the Faith & Family Foundation, laying the groundwork for what would become Wheatland Equestrian in Virginia. Their idea was built around a simple principle: riders with disabilities should have access to the same quality of coaching, competition and community as other riders. Over the years, the programme expanded from a small family-centred operation into an inclusive equestrian organisation serving riders with and without disabilities. Now, the historic property where that mission grew is taking on a different role, as its real estate value will support the organisation's long-term future. According to Wheatland Equestrian, the Forrests founded the Faith & Family Foundation in 1999, drawing on their own family experiences and Muriel's background with horses. The organisation's current programme has earned recognition as a USEF Para-Dressage Center of Excellence, while its former 43-acre Wheatland Farm property is being listed for approximately $8.4 million.A programme built around inclusionThe Forrests' motivation came partly from seeing how few sports and recreational opportunities were available to families raising children with disabilities. Muriel, who grew up with horses in Ireland, saw the physical, emotional and confidence-building benefits riding could provide. Wheatland Equestrian was created to bring families together rather than separating riders by ability. Its programme combines therapeutic riding, adapted riding, para-dressage and traditional equestrian training. Riders with disabilities, their siblings and non-disabled members of the community can train alongside one another.That approach has remained central to the organisation. As per Wheatland Equestrian, it now serves more than 100 riders each week across para-dressage, adapted riding, traditional dressage, eventing and youth programmes.From local programme to national recognitionThe organisation's development eventually took it into competitive para-equestrian sport. Wheatland Equestrian became the fourth centre nationwide to receive the USEF Para-Dressage Center of Excellence designation. Its former Wheatland Farm campus was equipped to support both recreational and high-level competition. The facilities included an FEI-quality outdoor competition arena, an ADA-compliant indoor arena, an accessible 18-stall barn with an automatic mounting lift for wheelchair-dependent athletes and outdoor trails. The organisation also hosted significant equestrian events, including a USEF 2018 Para Dressage Team Observation Event for the World Equestrian Games.A historic property with multiple usesThe farm itself is considerably more than an equestrian facility. The Crexi listing describes the property as a roughly 43-acre estate with about 41,522 square feet spread across eight structures. It includes a manor house, Wheatland Cottage, stables, indoor and outdoor riding arenas and an event centre. The property also has a long history. The Washington Business Journal reported that its manor house dates to 1741. The combination of historic buildings, equestrian infrastructure and its location in Loudoun County gives the property potential uses beyond its former nonprofit mission, including equestrian operations, events, retreats or a private compound.Turning property value into future servicesThe decision to sell does not represent an end to Wheatland Equestrian's work. The organisation has already moved to a new campus in Upperville, which it says is open and accepting students from Northern Virginia, Maryland and the Washington, D.C., area. According to Crexi, the sale is intended to convert the former campus's value into resources for the Faith & Family Foundation. The organisation sees the property as an appreciated asset that can provide an endowment and help support services for children and adults with disabilities and their families over the long term.That makes the sale more than a conventional real-estate transaction. The 43-acre farm that once provided the physical setting for Wheatland Equestrian's growth is now being positioned as a financial asset for its next chapter. Instead of keeping the organisation tied to a property that could limit future expansion, the proceeds can help sustain and potentially broaden its programmes. The farm's next owner may use its arenas, barns, historic buildings and acreage for an entirely different purpose. But for the Forrests and the Faith & Family Foundation, the property's next chapter is intended to continue the same broader mission that began in 1999: creating opportunities, community and support for people with disabilities and their families.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Islanders asked to report sightings of European eel in Guernsey
articles.summary: The Nature Commission asks people to record sightings of the critically endangered eels.
articles.body:
Islanders have been asked to record sightings of eels in a bid to help build a greater understanding of the fish.

Guernsey Nature Commission said there had been a 95% decline in the European eel population since the 1980s due largely to freshwater habitat loss and barriers to inland feeding grounds.

The International Union for Conservation of Nature's Red List of Threatened Species has registered the European eel a critically endangered species , the category closest to extinction.

Ecologist Charlotte Burgoine asked anyone with information on recent or historical sightings, or knowledge about areas in which eels used to be seen, to share it with the Nature Commission.

She said European eels had catadromous breeding, which meant they hatched in the Sargasso sea in the Atlantic Ocean, grew up in freshwater environments and then spawned back in the sea.

The eels are strong swimmers, emerge to hunt at night and, according to some sources, can live up to the age of 80, the ecologist added.

Burgoine said the Nature Commission and Guernsey Water were conducting environmental DNA sampling in the island's freshwater ponds and streams in a bid to gather more information as to where eels were present.

She said freshwater habitats were declining due to drainage and land clearance, habitat mismanagement and pollution.

"As such waterbodies are becoming more fragmented and isolated which may prevent eels from moving between them.

"Also, infrastructure along the coast and further inland, such as pipes and dams, makes it harder for returning eels to migrate inland to their feeding grounds," she added.

"These species are declining globally so it would be great to understand more about populations on island."
